script: My new coworker's wrath exploded—now I am stuck in a nightmare I can't escape.. I started my shift in a cramped floor with a dozen other cubicle‑mates. Every day we shuffled around a tiny room off the wall—just enough space for four, or six if we were friends. It was our unofficial conference room, the place where we could finally talk without the office buzz. Then Karl walked in. New guy, big ego, even bigger mouth. He'd boss anyone who'd look at him, hand off work like it was a favor, and claim his chair was too "bad for his back." He'd swap the old chair in his cubicle for someone else's, all while saying, "I am just helping." He'd borrow staples, coffee cups, his laptop. Basically, he owned the place. One day, I walk in and his cubicle is empty. Everything—his desk, his chair, his personal stuff—has been moved to that tiny room. He turned it into his office. We tried to talk, but he just shrugged, "First come, first served." He even slapped his name on a sign outside the door. That was the final straw. On the other end of the floor was a real conference room with a huge table, a screen, coffee station. We barely used it—just a few folks would pop in when it was free, ignoring the sign‑up sheet by the admin. Once a year we'd host a big meeting with folks from out of town. Karl, being the "meeting coordinator," took over the whole thing, keeping us out of the loop and driving the admin assistant nuts. When I learned the date, I booked the room. The admin whispered that Karl had a meeting that day, but he hadn't reserved it. She smirked, put my name on the sheet, and I was good. Five of us waited until Karl left the day before the meeting, then we hauled all our files, folders, and laptop cords into the conference room. We set up a PowerPoint, got the screen up, and started working at 8:00. The hallway buzzed, a voice announced the presentation, and we were in the zone. At 8:58, the door opened. Karl strutted in, surprised. People were peeking from behind him. He yanked us out, claiming he had important visitors and needed the room. We told him we'd booked it weeks ago, and that his "office" was no longer available. The briefer started again, but Karl stormed over to the admin's desk, yelling for the room. He talked for a minute, then returned and demanded we leave. "First come, first served," I said. He saw defeat. Karl's crew moved to a conference room upstairs. Our boss, who never even knew about the meeting, got a flood of harsh emails from the visitors. She was clueless about the whole mess. When she confronted Karl, she saw the evidence: his cubicle had been emptied, his "office" was a grab‑by‑force. He had to move back to his original cubicle. Revenge? Sweet, bestie.
